UCI World Championships 2026 Men’s Elite Road Race: Our form guide

Prepare yourself for one of the most wide open rainbow jersey fights in a long time. Defending champion Tadej Pogačar is out following his crash at the Vuelta a España, and plenty of riders will be relishing the opportunity to fight for the jersey in the men’s elite road race at the 2026 UCI World Championships.

Taking place in Montréal, Canada on Sunday 27th September, the 273.7km course begins in Brossard and eventually gets to a hilly 13.4km circuit around Mount Royal Park, which includes Voie Camillien-Houde (1.7km, 7.7%) and Côte de Polytechnique (0.8km, 5.7%). The riders will complete 12 laps to total 3,803m of elevation by the end, which is 200m more than the GP Montréal race, won this year by Isaac del Toro, which uses the same circuit but over a shorter 214.4km distance.

Isaac del Toro (Mexico)

He’s only 22 years old, but Mexico’s Isaac del Toro is the favourite here, cementing his status after winning the GP Montréal. Pogačar’s teammate and protégé, Del Toro will be relishing the opportunity to ride for himself here, especially without Pogačar to compete with. Having become the first Mexican to finish on the podium of the Tour de France in 2026, he could be the first to win here too.

He added a whole host of victories to his growing palmarès this year, including overall stage race wins at the UAE Tour, Tirreno-Adriatico and Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes. Unless something goes badly wrong, he will undoubtably improve on his seventh place on his elite race debut last year, the only question is: what colour will his medal be?

  • 7th: 2025

Paul Seixas (France)

The young riders are generating all the buzz this year. Like Del Toro, Frenchman Paul Seixas is having a meteoric rise, riding to fourth overall at the Tour on his debut this year. He was frequently best of the rest behind Pogačar in the hilly Classics in the spring, notching second places at Strade Bianche and Liège-Bastogne-Liège, and also won La Flèche Wallonne with its nasty kick uphill in the Muy de Huy to finish. He finished second behind Del Toro at the GP Montréal having been a solo leader before the Mexican caught him and beat him to the line.

Seixas bypassed the U23 rankings to finish 13th in the elite race on his first attempt last year having previously won an ITT gold medal in the junior Worlds in 2024.

Remco Evenepoel (Belgium)

Is the double on the cards? Belgium’s Remco Evenepoel just blitzed the field to claim his fourth consecutive elite individual time-trial gold medal and has won three of his last four races entered in the Donostia San Sebastian Klasikoa, Grand Prix Cyclist de Quebec and the Worlds ITT. This one-day form should serve him well as he hunts his first road race rainbows since 2022, and the first ever elite road and TT double. If anyone can do it it’s the double Olympic champion.

Mathieu van der Poel (Netherlands)

Mathieu van der Poel is in scintillating form, having just pulled off a successful 174km solo breakaway to win the final day at the Tour de Luxembourg. This summer he also won two stages at the Tour de France including the scintillating final stage in Paris.

The Classics extraordinaire raced to victory at Omloop Nieuwsblad and the E3 Saxo Classic this season but came second to Pogačar at the Tour of Flanders and finished just off the podium in Paris-Roubaix after a series of unfortunate mechanicals in the Arenberg forest. Van der Poel won road Worlds in Glasgow in 2023, but he should really be one to take advantage of a Pogačar-less race with this kind of parcours.

Tom Pidcock (Great Britain)

Freshly crowned MTB XCO World Champion Tom Pidcock is in great form, winning the GP Industria & Artigianato, finishing just off the podium at the GP Quebec and sixth at GP de Montréal in his first road races after MTB Worlds. Pidcock is a true one-day talent, despite his GC form over the past few years, and with cyclocross and MTB world titles to his name, this is the best opportunity he’ll get to add road to his set.

While he has a junior time-trial gold medal and bronze in the U23 road race to boast about, his best placing in the elite race came back in 2021 with sixth place.

Wout van Aert (Belgium)

This has been a great year for Wout van Aert. The Belgian finally won Paris-Roubaix, and took stages at the Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes and Tour of Denmark before a phenomenal Vuelta a España campaign that resulted in two wins for him and the points classification, plus five wins for teammate Matthew Brennan.

He has twice finished second in the World Championships road race. First to Julian Alaphilippe in 2020 and then to Van der Poel in 2023. A rainbow jersey would make this quite the season for Van Aert, though with Evenepoel on his team he won’t have a full squad of helpers – though having two cards to play may help.

Other contenders

This feels a very different rainbow jersey fight given the absence of Pogačar. It could well give us a surprise winner.

Ben Healy (Ireland) raced to a bronze medal last year and has a tenacity for a long, hard day in the saddle where he can go solo. Mauro Schmid (Switzerland) scored high placings in the Classics this year and won a stage at the Tour too, similarly if a move of outsiders gets clear he could certainly win. Quinn Simmons (United States) has had a fantastic season, with standout performances at the Tour de France, and more recently ninth at the Philadelphia Cycling Classic, fifth at the GP Quebec and fourth at the GP de Montréal, he’ll certainly be acclimatised to the time zone.

There’s also Juan Ayuso (Spain), Tobias Halland Johannessen (Norway), Christian Scaroni, Giulio Ciccone and Giulio Pellizzari (Italy), plus Florian Lipowitz (Germany) to keep an eye on. And it could be none of them – international racing often brings chaos.
